idiom_name: required keyword arguments + validation-before-assignment, private_class_method :new factory as Essence
implementation_notes: Ruby absorbs most of the classic two-class Essence structure: required keyword arguments in #initialize (def initialize(customer:, supplier:, start_date:)) make missing compulsory properties an ArgumentError naming the missing keywords, which is the presence half of Essence.validateParameters enforced by the language itself. Validation runs in #initialize before any assignment and raises before an instance exists, so an invalid object is never observable; attr_reader-only accessors plus freeze keep compulsory properties immutable after creation without a second class. For validation that should not live in the constructor, private_class_method :new hides the default constructor and a named factory class method (Contract.create) takes the Essence role: it validates parameters first and only then calls new, and it can build several related objects sharing the validated values. The classic form is still justified when construction involves external side effects or a staged interactive flow, where a separate collector object with explicit validateParameters feedback is clearer than a raise inside initialize.
code_sketch:
class Contract
  attr_reader :customer, :supplier, :start_date
  private_class_method :new

  def self.create(customer:, supplier:, start_date:)
    raise InvalidContract, 'customer required' if customer.nil? || customer.to_s.empty?
    raise InvalidContract, 'supplier required' if supplier.nil?
    new(customer:, supplier:, start_date:)
  end

  def initialize(customer:, supplier:, start_date:)
    @customer, @supplier, @start_date = customer, supplier, start_date
    freeze
  end
end
pitfalls: Ruby privacy is method-lookup convention, not access control: private_class_method :new only hides .new on that class - Object#send(:new) bypasses it and subclasses can re-publicize it, so the factory gate cannot stop a determined caller (the pattern's 'restrict constructor access' is weaker here than in C++/Java).

'missing keyword' ArgumentError only proves a value was passed, not that it is usable: callers can pass nil explicitly, blank strings are truthy, and Ruby has no non-null types - compulsory-ness therefore still needs explicit nil?/empty? guards, exactly the checks the Essence would have run.

Validation is not atomic with side effects: raising inside initialize leaves no object (good), but a factory that persists collaborators (e.g. saves a Supplier) before the Contract validation fails leaves partial state - run all validation before any side effect, not interleaved with construction.

freeze is shallow: a frozen Contract holding a mutable array of line items can still be mutated through the array (<< on the collection), so compulsory collections must be frozen (or duplicated and frozen) themselves.

Rescuing only ArgumentError conflates signature errors with domain rejections: without a dedicated domain exception (InvalidContract < StandardError), callers cannot distinguish 'you called the method wrong' from 'this contract violates a business rule'.
